title: Shadow of Intervention
text:
A learned-proxy measure of anticipated third-party intervention in civil conflicts
Theory predicts that anticipated third-party intervention shapes the calculus of rebellion — expected outside support can deter governments from repression or embolden opposition groups to fight. But no existing measure covers the full population of potential interveners, varies annually with shifting foreign policy alignments, or distinguishes government-biased from opposition-biased intervention. This project constructs one and uses it to test whether the shadow of intervention shapes civil war onset.

title: Shadow of Intervention
text:
The measure in practice



Government-biased (\(E^G\), solid) and opposition-biased (\(E^O\), dashed) intervention expectations for five countries, 1946–2014. Shaded bands mark civil war years.


The time series shows the measure behaving as theory predicts: intervention expectations vary meaningfully across countries and across time, tracking foreign policy realities rather than static structural features. Afghanistan’s government-side shadow spikes with Soviet involvement and again with post-2001 NATO presence; Angola’s opposition-side shadow rises sharply through its long civil conflict; Egypt shows asymmetric exposure across eras.
The regression result is clean in both direction and asymmetry: expected government intervention reduces civil war onset (coef = −2.39, SE = 0.53), expected opposition intervention increases it (coef = +1.69, SE = 0.54). The shadow subsumes both leading existing proxies and carries independent out-of-sample predictive content.

title: Shadow of Intervention
text:
Construction
The measure is built in two stages.
Stage 1 — Prediction. A super learner ensemble trained on the Regan (2000) dataset of military interventions (1946–2014) predicts, for each directed dyad in a given year, the probability and direction of intervention. The ensemble includes flexible nonparametric methods alongside the structural functional form implied by existing game-theoretic models; the structural model earns less than 1% of ensemble weight, meaning the data strongly prefer nonparametric alternatives.
Stage 2 — Aggregation. Dyad-level predictions are aggregated across all potential interveners to a country-year shadow, disciplined by a Nash fixed-point condition requiring each state’s predicted probability to be consistent as an input to the others’ predictions. The fixed-point is computationally tractable under a separability assumption; convergence is confirmed across all 25 imputation draws.

title: Shadow of Intervention
text:
Uncertainty
The learned-proxy approach has well-documented pitfalls: measurement-stage uncertainty is routinely ignored, and the disconnect between prediction and inference is papered over. This project follows Knox et al. (2022) closely. Measurement uncertainty is propagated into the regression via a two-stage pairs cluster bootstrap averaging across 25 imputation draws. The corrected standard errors are roughly 2.9–3.5× larger than naïve MLE output; approximately 88–92% of total coefficient variance originates in the measurement stage, not the regression. Standard errors that ignore this are not just conservative — they are wrong by nearly an order of magnitude.

title: Six’s Generals
text:
A data pipeline and quantitative analysis of French Revolutionary and Napoleonic military careers
Between 1789 and 1815, France transformed its army root and branch. The Old Regime had promoted officers by seniority and birth; the Revolution abolished those rules wholesale. Georges Six’s Dictionnaire biographique des généraux et amiraux français de la Révolution et de l’Empire (1934) records the result in extraordinary detail: 2,206 biographical entries, each a semicolon-delimited series of rank promotions, unit assignments, campaigns, wounds, and honors. The dictionary is, in effect, a longitudinal panel dataset in prose form.
This project converts Six’s prose into structured data and uses it to examine how military careers actually moved.

title: Six’s Generals
text:
Promotion speed across eras



Median years between consecutive single-step promotions, by rank and era. Green = fast; red = slow. Cells with fewer than five observations are blank.


Promotion times at every level of the hierarchy collapsed during the Revolution — the pre-Revolutionary median of roughly five years per step fell to about one year — then partially recovered under the Empire to roughly four years. The mechanism is over-determined: seniority rules abolished, the army expanding from 180,000 to over 700,000 men, performance displacing birth as the criterion for advancement. The data cannot separate these causes, but the scale of the shift is unambiguous.
One implication: if the Revolution was a structural shock, individual variation in promotion speed should be mostly noise. And it is. The correlation between consecutive wait times for the same general in the same era is r = 0.003 (p = 0.92) — the Revolution lifted all boats equally. The one exception is a within-Revolution correlation of r = 0.13 (p = 0.001), consistent with a modest merit-selection signal even within the accelerated environment.

title: Six’s Generals
text:
The pipeline
Six’s dictionary exists only as a poor-quality scan of a 1934 print publication. Converting it to structured data required building a full digitization pipeline from scratch.
The core challenges were not OCR — Marker handles the French text well — but structural. Six’s entries do not respect page boundaries: most pages begin mid-entry, and roughly half of all entries span two or more pages. The entry assembler detects boundaries using a two-pass regex strategy (ALL-CAPS surnames followed by parenthetical first-name blocks, with a fallback mixed-case pass for entries Six flagged as provisional), then stitches fragments across consecutive pages. Thirty-one pages required targeted manual corrections after automated assembly, each documented in the source.
Once assembled, each entry’s biographical prose is segmented into clauses and classified by type — rank promotion, unit assignment, campaign, honor, wound, administrative event — using a rule-based classifier tuned to Six’s consistent semicolon-delimited vocabulary. The classifier achieves a 13% residual unknown rate, down from 42% in its initial iteration, with no single unclassified pattern accounting for more than ~10 clauses.
Output: 2,208 biographical entries · 88,282 classified clauses · 52-column rectangular export

title: Six’s Generals
text:
Further analysis
The structured dataset supports a range of additional questions covered in the full analysis document: geographic origins of the officer corps; Arc de Triomphe inscriptions and their relationship to Napoleon’s personal presence at engagements; army assignments and career roles; post-career pensions; and the imperial honor economy.

title: D-SOCIAL-KLD
text: Dynamic IRT scores for corporate social responsibility · 1991–2018 · with David Primo and Brian Kelleher Richter

title: D-SOCIAL-KLD
text:
Overview
KLD STATS (now MSCI ESG) codes publicly traded U.S. firms on dozens of binary indicators each year — strengths and concerns across categories like environment, labor, governance, and community relations. The standard approach in the management literature is the KLD Index: sum the strengths and subtract the concerns. This treats every indicator as equally informative, which is a strong and usually implausible assumption.
D-SOCIAL-KLD replaces the additive index with a dynamic two-parameter IRT model. The model treats firms as examinees and KLD indicators as test items. A discrimination parameter for each item lets the data decide how informative each indicator is; a difficulty parameter captures how demanding each indicator is at the population level. A firm-specific random walk prior links scores across years, encoding the intuition that a firm’s CSR position in 2006 is strongly predicted by its position in 2005.
The result is a posterior distribution over a latent CSR score \(\theta_{it}\) for each firm-year — with uncertainty quantified, discrimination weights estimated from the data, and year-to-year dynamics modeled explicitly.

title: D-SOCIAL-KLD
text:
The model
\[
y_{ijt} \sim \text{Bernoulli}\bigl(\Phi(\beta_{jt} \cdot \theta_{it} - \alpha_{jt})\bigr)
\]

\(\theta_{it}\): latent CSR score for firm \(i\) in year \(t\)
\(\alpha_{jt}\): difficulty of indicator \(j\) in year \(t\)
\(\beta_{jt}\): discrimination of indicator \(j\) in year \(t\)
Year-to-year dynamics: \(\theta_{i,t} = \theta_{i,t-1} + \sigma_{\text{firm},i} \cdot \varepsilon\)

Estimation uses Stan’s No-U-Turn Sampler with a non-centered parameterization for the dynamic prior, which resolves the funnel geometry that the centered form creates in the joint posterior.

title: D-SOCIAL-KLD
text:
Data

Source: KLD STATS, 1991–2018, via Wharton Research Data Services
Coverage: ~6,300 unique firms; 2,000+ indicator-year items; ~1.5M non-missing observations
Universe: firms present in the KLD database by 2012 (for comparability with published scores)

title: D-SOCIAL-KLD
text:
Outputs
The estimation pipeline produces posterior means, standard deviations, and percentiles for:

Firm-year scores (\(\theta_{it}\)): the primary quantity of interest
Item parameters (\(\alpha_{jt}\), \(\beta_{jt}\)): difficulty and discrimination for each indicator-year

Scores are interval-scaled and centered near zero in each year. Posterior uncertainty is reported explicitly and should be propagated into downstream analyses.

KLD rates firms on dozens of binary ESG indicators each year. Rather than summing them into an index, this project estimates a latent CSR score for each firm-year using a dynamic two-parameter IRT model fit in Stan. Georges Six’s Dictionnaire biographique (1934) contains structured biographical entries for every general and admiral of Revolutionary and Imperial France.
